title: Al Klink, Glenn Miller solos and repeating recorded solos
summary: Al Klink's time with Miller and his solo on In the Mood; whether recorded solos were worked out and replayed.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Wasn’t Al Klink — was he one of the fellows with the Goodman orchestra — no, I mean Glenn Miller?

Yes. Virtually I don’t think he was really a charter member. I mean he was with the group early on when then just began to be so successful, and in those busy years when they were doing the Paramount Theater in New York and the Chesterfield Show and the Pennsylvania Hotel, and some of them simultaneously. They’d finish a broadcast and there’d be cabs lined up waiting to take them to the Pennsylvania Hotel so they could
play a show. Yeah, Al became a very close friend. He’s on the first three LPs I ever made.
He’s probably one of the guys that did one of those famous tenor solos on “In The Mood.”
Yeah, that’s Al. That’s the only solo I think he ever recorded in the Glenn Miller band.
Tex of course was the soloist, and he was the personality that Glenn Miller was trying to develop, and he did so successfully. But he and Al were very close friends.

I’ve always wondered sometimes, those solos from the Miller recordings, if they were improvised at the time. Because they became like THE solo to play. They actually would write them out, they were written out in the arrangements.

I suppose later on they were, but I think at the time, when they knew they were going to make a record of a particular tune, and they had a solo, they would work out a solo, play it on the record, and maybe play it from then on, which I don’t think is all that bad really. I mean if it was good enough to play on the record, why not play it a few times more? I mean I don’t think it would be good to do it year on end, in fact I think that’s why Artie Shaw got out of the business. Because how many times can I play that chorus on “Stardust” and mean it? I mean I’m not quoting anybody, I’m just — I think.
